name: Rhodiola rosea
lead: Rhodiola rosea, known as golden root, rose root or Arctic root, is a perennial succulent in the stonecrop family (Crassulaceae) that grows in cold, high-altitude and Arctic regions of Europe, Asia and North America.[1][2] Its rhizome is used in traditional medicine and sold as an adaptogen: a supplement promoted for stress, fatigue and stamina.[1][2]

The rhizome contains roughly 140 compounds, including the phenylpropanoids rosavin, rosarin and rosin and the phenylethanoid salidroside.[1] A 2010 review summarised its traditional use, chemistry and clinical efficacy, and laboratory work on salidroside reports neuroprotective, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects in cells and animals.[2][3][4][5]

Wikipedia states that researchers have found no high-quality clinical evidence that the plant treats any disease, and cites a 2012 European Medicines Agency report that described published trials as having considerable quality deficiencies.[1] No study found in these sources tests rhodiola for appearance outcomes.

paras: Wikipedia reports the plant has a history in traditional medicine and is sold in Asia and Eastern Europe as capsules, liquid extracts and tablets; Pedanius Dioscorides described it in De Materia Medica and Carl Linnaeus later named it.[1] The 2010 Phytomedicine review covers its traditional use in Scandinavia, Russia and Asia, and a 1999 paper grouped it with other adaptogenic herbs in Ayurvedic and related medicine.[2][6]

Salidroside is the most studied constituent in the laboratory. Cell and animal studies report that it protects neuroblastoma cells against oxidative and amyloid-induced injury,[7][8] stimulates the Sirt1/PGC-1 alpha axis in a mouse diabetic-nephropathy model,[9] and inhibits inflammatory signalling in psoriasis-related and endothelial cell models.[4][10] Wikipedia notes that rosavin, rosarin, rosin and salidroside have no demonstrated physiological effect in humans.[1] A 2011 review of herbal medicines for depression, anxiety and insomnia discusses rhodiola among the herbs examined.[11]

The 2010 review assessed clinical studies, mainly of fatigue, stress and mood, and Wikipedia cites the EMA's 2012 conclusion that published trials showed considerable deficiencies in quality.[2][1] Registered trials include studies of Rhodiola crenulata in COPD (57) and in acute mountain sickness (125),[12][13] adults with ADHD (two Phase 4 studies of 60 each),[14][15] mental and physical fatigue (90),[16] and several small exercise and cognition studies in athletes and healthy adults (13 to 27 participants).[17][18] The sources consulted give no results for these, and none tests a cosmetic or appearance outcome.

Wikipedia states the US FDA has issued warning letters to supplement makers over unapproved health claims for rhodiola, including claims about Raynaud syndrome, altitude sickness, depression and cancer.[1] The plant is listed under CITES Appendix II, and demand has led to overharvesting of wild populations and to adulteration of products.[1] A US homeopathic-style adrenal product label lists rhodiola among its ingredients with advice to consult a professional if pregnant or breastfeeding.[19]

lore.intro: On looksmaxxing forums rhodiola appears mainly in questions about productivity supplements and hormonal side effects rather than as an appearance compound.[20]

claims.claim: Rhodiola may affect estrogen and testosterone
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster asking about safety said they had read online that rhodiola has effects on estrogen and testosterone and worried this could harm their looksmaxxing, given an existing hormonal imbalance.[20]
claims.experts: The reviews and regulatory statements summarised in the sources consulted focus on fatigue, stress and mood, and Wikipedia reports no high-quality evidence of clinical effects; no human hormone-focused study is cited there.[1][2]

claims.claim: Anything that boosts productivity abruptly is best avoided, like energy drinks
claims.believers: A reply in the same thread likened such supplements to energy drinks and advised avoiding them.[20]
claims.experts: Reviews describe rhodiola as an adaptogen with modest or inconsistent trial results, and the EMA noted deficiencies in published trial quality.[1][2]

card.summary: The Arctic adaptogen root sold for stress and fatigue; mixed-quality trials and nothing on appearance.
card.aka: Golden root, rose root, Arctic root, Rhodiola
card.note: FDA warning letters issued over unapproved health claims; wild populations are overharvested.

quick.overview:
Rhodiola rosea is an Arctic and mountain succulent whose root is sold as an adaptogen for stress, fatigue and stamina. Forum mentions focus on productivity and worries about hormones.

A 2010 review summarised its clinical efficacy, but Wikipedia cites an EMA report describing the published trials as having considerable quality deficiencies. No trial tests appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: Its rosavins and salidroside are reported in cell and animal studies to have antioxidant, neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory activity, including via Sirt1 signalling.
quick.risks: FDA has issued warning letters over unapproved claims. The plant is listed under CITES Appendix II and products can be adulterated. Wikipedia does not discuss human adverse effects, and no study cited here examines hormone effects.
